arXiv|arxiv:2609.23889.title: SyzHarness: Patch-Based Kernel Bug Reproduction with LLM-Synthesized Fuzzing Harnesses
arXiv|arxiv:2609.23889.abstract: Automated kernel vulnerability reproduction is essential for bug triage, patch validation, and regression testing, but still lacks an effective and efficient solution. The core challenge is twofold: a reproducer must first recover the trigger scaffold needed to reach the vulnerable state and determine the precise concrete values that actually trigger the bug. Existing directed fuzzing approaches are ineffective at recovering the necessary trigger scaffold, while LLM-only generation is brittle because it struggles with concrete-value discovery and runtime nondeterminism. We design SyzHarness, a framework that combines LLM reasoning with coverage-guided fuzzing for patch-based Linux kernel vulnerability reproduction. Given a patch, SyzHarness uses an LLM agent grounded by code navigation tools to synthesize a parameterized fuzzing harness that fixes the prerequisite setup logic while exposing only uncertain, bug-critical input parameters to be mutated by Syzkaller. SyzHarness then translates this harness into a Syzkaller compatible interface and iteratively refines it using hierarchical reachability feedback. We evaluate SyzHarness on multiple datasets of triggerable real-world Linux kernel vulnerabilities. On 100 KernelCTF cases, SyzHarness achieves a 78% bug reproduction success rate. On the SyzDirect benchmark, SyzHarness achieves a 73% bug reproduction success rate, substantially outperforming prior directed greybox fuzzing. On 50 recent, known-triggerable syzbot bugs fixed after March 2026, SyzHarness reproduces 40/50 (80%) using only the fix commits as input.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.26007.title: System-One RSI: Building Muscle Memory for Interactive Agents through Guided Practice
arXiv|arxiv:2611.26007.abstract: Reasoning models provide strong multimodal task understanding but struggle with sub-second control because deliberation increases decision latency. Fast decision models can meet the response window, yet prompting and few-shot examples do not readily provide the fine-grained experience required by a new task. Inspired by coached motor learning, this paper presents System-One Recursive Self-Improvement (System-One RSI), which couples two loops. The high-frequency online inner loop is an Observe, Orient, Decide, Act (OODA) cycle: a decision model maps each visual observation and task question to structured judgments, and a decision tree converts them into timed actions without invoking a reasoning model. The offline outer loop is a recursive improvement cycle carried out by a team of reasoning agents. The team revises the decision-model prompt and decision tree, captures interaction records, derives supervision from those records, and trains or deploys updated model parameters. The improved system then returns to the environment and generates the experience for the next round, consolidating learned distinctions as external muscle memory. The framework operates with a small number of real episodes, without expert demonstrations, environment modification, sandboxing, or parallel simulation. Experiments in Snake, Zenless Zone Zero, and Black Myth: Wukong use a 27B decision model. Mean Snake score increases from 1.30 to 7.35. In an evaluated scenario of Zenless Zone Zero, median completion time decreases by 8.4%. In an evaluated combat scenario of Black Myth: Wukong, the evasive policy achieves 11 times the mean survival time of a stationary reference, while the offensive policy win rate rises from 0% to 66.7% across the evaluated configurations.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.16039.title: When Agents Talk, Secrets Travel: Topology-Driven Leakage and Recipient-Conditioned Sanitization in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
arXiv|arxiv:2610.16039.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems (MALS) introduce a privacy-leakage problem that conventional sensitivity-based defenses miss, since information disclosed to one authorized agent can propagate through routine coordination to an unauthorized one, without compromise or malicious behavior. This motivates topology-aware enforcement that blocks unauthorized propagation while preserving authorized disclosure. We evaluate 485 scenarios across coordinator-worker, peer-to-peer, and hierarchical topologies, instrumenting seven communication channels and measuring surface leakage and disclosure to topology-introduced recipients. We introduce RECONS, a Detect -> Decide -> Transform sanitizer conditioning intervention on recipient and execution context rather than sensitivity alone. Topology changes where protected information propagates, with disclosure to topology-introduced recipients rising from 0% to 52.2% while surface leakage stays nearly flat at 60.6-62.8%. This effect persists across four generator models and a second orchestration framework, though magnitude and relay paths differ; framework choice separately drives a 150x leakage spread, so topology alone is not sufficient. RECONS reduces residual disclosure from 96.7% without sanitization to 29.25%, preserving 94.1% of authorized disclosures versus 20.5% under blanket redaction. Detection coverage is the dominant bottleneck, accounting for 95.5% of residual disclosures. These results show that privacy enforcement in MALS must reason about the recipient and communication path realized at runtime, not sensitivity or topology assumptions alone.

arXiv|arxiv:2609.29672.title: LLMersion: A Local-First AI Agent Framework for Low-Cost Home Language Learning toward Educational Equity
arXiv|arxiv:2609.29672.abstract: Artificial intelligence helps education most where an essential provision has been rationed by cost. For language learners that provision is a teacher's voice, which binds listening, reading, speaking, and writing into one act. Published evidence shows why most learners lack it, from a global shortage of 44 million teachers to heavy household tutoring bills, and why technology has not substituted for it: computer-assisted language learning proved effective but narrow, applications presuppose connectivity 2.6 billion people lack, and One Laptop per Child's randomized evaluation found that hardware without capable software teaches nothing. We distill eight difficulties and four binding constraints, and argue that small open-weight models dissolve the last: a complete four-skill stack now fits a \$200-class laptop and, on community measurements, generates at the pace speech is consumed, for about one US cent of electricity per study hour. We therefore propose LLMersion, a scheme for AI for education that runs entirely at home, over the learner's own documents, with an AI-written, AI-understood, AI-updated codebase anyone can customize; present LLMersion-1, a released open-source prototype (https://github.com/QM378/LLMersion ); and outline the vision of a private learning agent.

ACL Anthology|https://aclanthology.org/2.title: Layer-Order Inversion: Rethinking Latent Multi-Hop Reasoning in Large Language Models
ACL Anthology|https://aclanthology.org/2.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform well on multi-hop reasoning, yet how they internally compose multiple facts remains unclear. Recent work proposes hop-aligned circuit hypothesis, suggesting that bridge entities are computed sequentially across layers before later-hop answers. Through systematic analyses on real-world multi-hop queries, we show that this hop-aligned assumption does not generalize: later-hop answer entities can become decodable earlier than bridge entities, a phenomenon we call layer-order inversion, which strengthens with total hops. To explain this behavior, we propose a probabilistic recall-and-extract framework that models multi-hop reasoning as broad probabilistic recall in shallow MLP layers followed by selective extraction in deeper attention layers. Through probing and causal intervention analyses, we further show that shallow recall of deeper-hop knowledge can act as an intuition-like signal for answer selection, with stronger effects in weaker models and higher-hop queries. Our framework further explains prior empirical phenomena and provides a mechanistic diagnosis of multi-hop failures despite correct single-hop knowledge. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Layer-Order-Inversion/.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.23225.title: StringQFT: A Multiuse Textbook Resource for AI-Assisted Theoretical Physics
arXiv|arxiv:2611.23225.abstract: We present StringQFT as a textbook collection for string constructions of quantum field theory and as infrastructure for AI-assisted theoretical physics. The collection comprises 18 volumes, 190 chapters and 3,795 pages, covering brane probes, brane webs, geometric engineering, F-theory constructions, wrapped M5-branes and exact worldsheet constructions. Its open-book benchmark inventory contains 1,073 items, including 499 with automatic finite-answer checking. For retrieval-augmented generation, it provides 1,371 section records linked to textbook sources and PDF locations, together with a local lexical retriever. Training-data preparation is illustrated by 21 private, source-linked examples. For agents, it exposes 19 calculation tools with specified inputs and finite domains, connecting tool use to textbook derivations. We illustrate these uses through specific questions, retrieved passages and finite calculations. The textbook collection and accompanying resources are available at https://github.com/xingyang-yu/StringQFT.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.24537.title: Write Once, Query Many: Evolving Compact Reusable Memory for Long Videos
arXiv|arxiv:2610.24537.abstract: Long videos often exceed the context capacity of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), while agentic search repeats costly video processing and grounding for each query. Reusable memory can amortize this cost, but must preserve information for questions unknown during construction. We propose Video-EMem, an evolvable video memory harness built on time-anchored perceptual observations. This representation combines compact free-form text with sparse images to preserve semantic content and complementary visual details across temporal scales, supporting temporal navigation without a fixed semantic schema. A Writer encodes each video once by consolidating overlapping multiscale observations, and a Reader retrieves and organizes evidence solely from the resulting memory. With the underlying models frozen, we evolve their workflows and operators using distinct feedback: query-independent source fidelity and coverage for the Writer, and QA failures in evidence localization and utilization for the Reader. Experiments support this separation for generalization beyond development queries, with our evolution strategy improving average accuracy by 7.2% over the unevolved harness. While reducing storage by about 99.86% on average relative to raw videos, Video-EMem improves Qwen3-VL-30B by an average of 2.6% across three long-video QA benchmarks over direct input of 2,048 frames. Using the same o3 answer model as the state-of-the-art agentic method, it improves average accuracy by 2.5% with lower per-query latency.

arXiv|arxiv:2606.18557.title: DeFAb: A Dataset for Grounded Scientific Discovery through Defeasible Abduction
arXiv|arxiv:2606.18557.abstract: A theory can accommodate a counterexample by adding an exception. The harder problem is deciding how far the exception should extend and which predictions should survive. We present DeFAb, a dataset and symbolic verification framework built from curated biological knowledge in the Gene Ontology. Models fill gaps in a theory or propose exceptions to its rules. A verifier checks the consequences of each edit, allowing different solutions to receive credit. Simple symbolic repairs solve all 336 tasks in the released evaluation panel. This result exposes a limitation of the revision test. An exception tied to one entity can succeed without identifying a pattern that applies to other cases. We develop a contextual task that requires an exception to reach the relevant cases and preserve predictions elsewhere. Two planned studies compare training with verified and rejected examples, and revision with and without feedback about consequences. DeFAb makes the scope of a proposed explanation testable, providing a controlled step toward studying theory revision in scientific reasoning.

OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.title: SceneWeaver: All-in-One 3D Scene Synthesis with an Extensible and Self-Reflective Agent
OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: Indoor scene synthesis has become increasingly important with the rise of Embodied AI, which requires 3D environments that are not only visually realistic but also physically plausible and functionally diverse. While recent approaches have advanced visual fidelity, they often remain constrained to fixed scene categories, lack sufficient object-level detail and physical consistency, and struggle to align with complex user instructions. In this work, we present SceneWeaver, a reflective agentic framework that unifies diverse scene synthesis paradigms through tool-based iterative refinement. At its core, SceneWeaver employs a language model-based planner to select from a suite of extensible scene generation tools, ranging from data-driven generative models to visual- and LLM-based methods, guided by self-evaluation of physical plausibility, visual realism, and semantic alignment with user input. This closed-loop reason-act-reflect design enables the agent to identify semantic inconsistencies, invoke targeted tools, and update the environment over successive iterations. Extensive experiments on both common and open-vocabulary room types demonstrate that \model not only outperforms prior methods on physical, visual, and semantic metrics, but also generalizes effectively to complex scenes with diverse instructions, marking a step toward general-purpose 3D environment generation.

PMLR|https://proceedings.mlr.press/v306/.title: PRISM: Distribution-free Adaptive Computation of Matrix Functions for Accelerating Neural Network Training
PMLR|https://proceedings.mlr.press/v306/.abstract: Matrix functions such as square root, inverse roots, and orthogonalization play a central role in preconditioned gradient methods for neural network training. This has motivated the development of iterative algorithms that avoid explicit eigendecompositions and rely primarily on matrix multiplications, making them well suited for modern GPU accelerators. We present PRISM (Polynomial-fitting and Randomized Iterative Sketching for Matrix functions computation), a general framework for accelerating iterative algorithms for computing matrix functions. PRISM combines adaptive polynomial approximation with randomized sketching: at each iteration, it fits a polynomial surrogate to the current spectrum via a sketched least-squares problem, adapting to the instance at hand with minimal overhead. We apply PRISM to accelerate Newton–Schulz-like iterations for matrix square roots and orthogonalization, which are core primitives in machine learning. Unlike prior methods, PRISM requires no explicit spectral bounds or singular value estimates; it adapts automatically to the evolving spectrum. Empirically, PRISM accelerates training when integrated into Shampoo and Muon optimizers.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.19155.title: FACT: A Multimodal Force-Action-Track Foundation Model for Human-to-Robot Dexterity
arXiv|arxiv:2610.19155.abstract: Human demonstrations offer a scalable alternative to costly robot data collection for dexterous manipulation, but most human datasets lack force measurements. Dexterous manipulation requires not only visual and proprioceptive understanding but also the ability to anticipate and regulate interaction forces. To scale force-aware human-robot co-training, we introduce EgoForce, a large-scale human tactile dataset capturing force-rich manipulation experience, and combine it with robot demonstrations for pretraining. We present FACT, a robot foundation model that cascades from prospective visual planning to force-aware refinement for dexterous manipulation. FACT comprises two jointly trained components. A Track-Guided Coarse Planner jointly predicts actions, future video, and visual tracks. Future video and visual tracks also provide a shared task representation that facilitates cross-embodiment knowledge transfer and coarse action generation. Building on this coarse plan, a Force-Action Joint Refiner jointly predicts future force and refines the coarse action, allowing anticipated force and action to shape each other during refinement. We evaluate the model on ten tasks requiring fine-grained coordination and force feedback, including tool use, musical instruments, and precision laboratory procedures. Using as few as 10 robot trajectories with 90 human trajectories for fine-tuning, FACT outperforms both baselines, with success-rate gains of up to 60 percentage points over T-Rex. Ablations show that force supervision in human pretraining data is crucial for downstream robot performance after fine-tuning, while visual track prediction and training with future-force prediction improve dexterous execution. Experiments varying the human-robot data ratio during fine-tuning further suggest that FACT learns from human demonstrations nearly as effectively as from robot demonstrations.

arXiv|arxiv:2512.24205.title: Micro-Macro Tensor Neural Surrogates for Uncertainty Quantification in Collisional Plasma
arXiv|arxiv:2512.24205.abstract: Plasma kinetic equations exhibit pronounced sensitivity to microscopic perturbations in model parameters and data, making reliable and efficient uncertainty quantification (UQ) essential for predictive simulations. However, the cost of uncertainty sampling, the high-dimensional phase space, and multiscale stiffness pose severe challenges to both computational efficiency and error control in traditional numerical methods. These aspects are further emphasized in presence of collisions where the high-dimensional nonlocal collision integrations and conservation properties pose severe constraints. To overcome this, we present a variance-reduced Monte Carlo framework for UQ in the Vlasov--Poisson--Landau (VPL) system, in which neural network surrogates replace the multiple costly evaluations of the Landau collision term. The method couples a high-fidelity, asymptotic-preserving VPL solver with inexpensive, strongly correlated surrogates based on the Vlasov--Poisson--Fokker--Planck (VPFP) and Euler--Poisson (EP) equations. For the surrogate models, we introduce a generalization of the separable physics-informed neural network (SPINN), developing a class of tensor neural networks based on an anisotropic micro-macro decomposition, to reduce velocity-moment costs, model complexity, and the curse of dimensionality. To further increase correlation with VPL, we calibrate the VPFP model and design an asymptotic-preserving SPINN whose small- and large-Knudsen limits recover the EP and VP systems, respectively. Numerical experiments show substantial variance reduction over standard Monte Carlo, accurate statistics with far fewer high-fidelity samples, and lower wall-clock time, while maintaining robustness to stochastic dimension.

arXiv|arxiv:2609.19814.title: Long-horizon autoformalization of a core theorem underlying MIP* = RE
arXiv|arxiv:2609.19814.abstract: Landmark mathematical formalizations have taken specialist teams years to complete. We present FormalFlow, a system that coordinates AI proving agents under human supervision to address statement drift and proof composition in long-horizon formalization. Drawing on software-engineering principles and practices, it uses a shared blueprint to guide nested planning, proving, and review loops. Using FormalFlow, we completed a machine-checked Lean 4 proof of the quantum soundness of the classical low individual-degree test, a core theorem underlying MIP* = RE, in 63 days. The final library contains 126,367 lines of Lean code, all generated by agents. Beyond providing a verified foundation for quantum complexity, the formalization corrects side conditions and intermediate error bounds in the published proof and improves the error exponent of the main theorem. The development record shows what it takes to trust proofs written by AI agents and provides reusable tools for verifying research mathematics at scale.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.16281.title: RelLedger: Relational Information Governance for LLM Agent Organizations
arXiv|arxiv:2610.16281.abstract: In LLM agent organizations, shared records determine which facts are available for later decisions. A sender consults interaction histories before deciding whether to report an event. A delivery gap across histories does not show whose relationship drove the choice or whether the resulting record matters downstream. We introduce RelLedger to audit these links. It holds the event, evidence, risk, and message fixed while crossing the sender's histories with the event target and an unrelated actor. Role reassignment and history rewrites locate the controlling cue. Message and cost interventions show when the effect appears. An attribution ledger maps each claim to its required response cells and separates missing interventions from sampling uncertainty. Recipient replay follows delivered information into downstream decisions. Executable workflows for a simulated one-person company extend the audit to retrieved histories, tool calls, and shared ledger updates. Across GPT, Gemini, Claude, DeepSeek, and Qwen, the audit reveals model-specific control paths and smaller relation gaps under explicit loss rules. Claude sends the same factual notice 62.22 percentage points more often with conflict histories than with friendly histories. In executable workflows, strained histories reduce recipient review rates by 45.83 points relative to warm histories for Claude.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.22379.title: When is a large language model a good calibration agent? Physics-labeled prompting for budgeted engineering simulator calibration
arXiv|arxiv:2610.22379.abstract: Calibrating expensive engineering simulators requires tuning model parameters to match reference data, a process heavily constrained by computational costs. This study investigates whether Large Language Models (LLMs), conditioned on physical diagnostic descriptions of simulation errors, can propose informative parameter updates more efficiently than conventional derivative-free optimizers. We test this on a cylinder-wake Large-Eddy Simulation and a damped-oscillator inverse problem. Physics-labeled prompts are evaluated against four text ablations (removed, anonymized, padded, misdirected) and standard optimizers (Nelder-Mead, Bayesian optimization, CMA-ES, and random search). Results demonstrate a strong early semantic advantage: the first physics-informed LLM proposal improves the initial design in 23 of 25 trials. After five evaluations, the median calibration error is 21.9 times lower than physics-free controls. However, this advantage is transient - disappearing by fifteen evaluations - and inherent LLM decoder variability yields a 9.8-fold performance spread. To address this, we introduce a hybrid workflow that uses the LLM as a warm-start, passing accumulated evaluations to a conventional optimizer. This two-stage numerical continuation policy reaches target accuracy in just 9 simulator runs, outperforming the LLM alone (12 runs), Nelder-Mead (17 runs), and Bayesian optimization (>60 runs). Supported by sensitivity analysis validating the test cases, this hybrid physics-labeled LLM scheme proves highly effective as a calibration agent under strict evaluation budgets.

arXiv|arxiv:2603.08393.title: Decoupling Distance and Networks: Hybrid Graph Attention-Geostatistical Methods for Spatio-temporal Risk Mapping
arXiv|arxiv:2603.08393.abstract: Accurate spatial prediction and rigorous uncertainty quantification are central to modern spatial epidemiology and environmental risk analysis. We introduce a statistically principled hybrid modelling framework that integrates the nonlinear, attention-based representation learning capabilities of a dynamic Graph Attention Network (GATv2) with a latent Gaussian spatial process from model-based geostatistics (MBG). This framework jointly captures relational dependence encoded in graph structures and continuous spatial dependence governed by physical proximity. We evaluate the proposed model via a controlled simulation study and an applied analysis of malaria prevalence data, comparing its predictive accuracy, calibration, and uncertainty quantification against classical geostatistical models and standalone GATv2 architectures. Our analyses show that GATv2 captures complex nonlinear interactions but fails to account for residual spatial autocorrelation, resulting in miscalibrated predictive distributions. Conversely, geostatistical models provide coherent uncertainty quantification through structured covariance functions yet are constrained by linear predictor assumptions and by their reliance on Euclidean distance to encode spatial structure. By integrating attention mechanisms and nonlinear features with an explicit probabilistic spatial random field, the hybrid model captured the relational dependence, consistently improved predictive accuracy, and provided more realistic uncertainty quantification in both simulation and applied settings. Overall, the findings demonstrate that the hybrid model constitutes a statistically coherent and empirically robust framework for modelling complex spatial and spatio-temporal processes in settings where both distance-based and structure-based dependencies operate.

arXiv|arxiv:2606.06473.title: MLEvolve: A Self-Evolving Framework for Automated Machine Learning Algorithm Discovery
arXiv|arxiv:2606.06473.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly applied to long-horizon tasks such as scientific discovery and machine learning engineering (MLE), where sustained self-evolution becomes a key capability. However, existing MLE agents suffer from isolated exploration, inefficient experience reuse, and lack of hierarchical control, which together hinder long-horizon optimization. We present MLEvolve, an LLM-based self-evolving multi-agent framework for end-to-end machine learning algorithm discovery. By extending tree search to Progressive MCGS, MLEvolve enables cross-branch information flow through graph-based reference edges and gradually shifts the search from broad exploration to focused exploitation with an entropy-inspired progressive schedule. To allow the agent to evolve with accumulated experience, we introduce Retrospective Memory, which combines a cold-start domain knowledge base with a dynamic global memory for task-specific experience retrieval and reuse. For stable long-horizon iteration, we further decouple strategic planning from code generation with adaptive coding modes. Evaluation on MLE-Bench shows that MLEvolve achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple dimensions including average medal rate and valid submission rate under a 12-hour budget (half the standard runtime). Moreover, MLEvolve also outperforms specialized algorithm discovery methods including AlphaEvolve on mathematical algorithm optimization tasks, demonstrating strong cross-domain generalization. Code is available at https://github.com/InternScience/MLEvolve.

arXiv|arxiv:2311.08908.title: Robust Brain MRI Image Classification with SIBOW-SVM
arXiv|arxiv:2311.08908.abstract: Primary Central Nervous System tumors in the brain are among the most aggressive diseases affecting humans. Early detection and classification of brain tumor types, whether benign or malignant, glial or non-glial, is critical for cancer prevention and treatment, ultimately improving human life expectancy. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is the most effective technique for brain tumor detection, generating comprehensive brain scans. However, human examination can be error-prone and inefficient due to the complexity, size, and location variability of brain tumors. Recently, automated classification techniques using machine learning methods, such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), have demonstrated significantly higher accuracy than manual screening. However, deep learning-based image classification methods, including CNNs, face challenges in estimating class probabilities without proper model calibration. In this paper, we propose a novel brain tumor image classification method called SIBOW-SVM, which integrates the Bag-of-Features model with SIFT feature extraction and weighted Support Vector Machines. This new approach can effectively extract hidden image features, enabling differentiation of various tumor types, provide accurate label predictions, and estimate probabilities of images belonging to each class, offering high-confidence classification decisions. We have also developed scalable and parallelable algorithms to facilitate the practical implementation of SIBOW-SVM for massive image datasets. To benchmark our method, we apply SIBOW-SVM to a public dataset of brain tumor MRI images containing four classes: glioma, meningioma, pituitary, and normal. Our results demonstrate that the new method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques, including CNNs, in terms of uncertainty quantification, classification accuracy, computational efficiency, and data robustness.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.31319.title: Conformalized Tree-Based Gradient Ensembles for Out-of-Distribution Detection and Plausible Recourse
arXiv|arxiv:2611.31319.abstract: Counterfactual recourse provides actionable feature adjustments that reverse unfavourable predictions made by automated decision models. However, when recourse search optimizes purely against classifier confidence or narrow proxy scores over gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDT), search procedures can exploit boundary artifacts and low-density regions---an instance of Goodhart's law---yielding out-of-distribution (OOD) recommendations that appear favourable nominally while lacking manifold plausibility. In this paper, we study conformalized OOD gating coupled with actionability-constrained counterfactual search across two tabular benchmarks: Adult and Give Me Some Credit (GMSC). Calibrating finite-sample anomaly gates (gate_IF, gate_LOF, and the conjunctive gate_ALL) at significance level delta = 0.05 over isolation forest, local outlier factor, and k-nearest-neighbor signals, we audit generated counterfactuals against held-out GMM and OCSVM detectors alongside ablation studies (gen10, gen100, and relax). Across matched recourse pairs where both constrained and unconstrained searches succeed, gate_ALL significantly reduces held-out OCSVM flags on Adult (N=541, Delta flag_OCSVM = -0.0296, p_Holm = 4.0e-4) and lowers both held-out flags on GMSC (N=540, Delta flag_OCSVM = -0.0346, p = 1.0751e-4; Delta flag_GMM = -0.1663, p = 3.5679e-16) while increasing matched recourse cost (Delta cost = +0.3035, p = 1.3365e-5) and narrowing overall feasibility. Our findings formalize the cost--feasibility--plausibility trade-off and demonstrate how conformal OOD gating audits recourse reliability on tabular ensembles.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.25071.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) write fluent financial analyses but miscompute ratios, recall stale prices, and route questions to the wrong tool with high confidence. We ask which component should do each job in a financial question-answering assistant, and study it with FinVeriQA, an open-source multi-agent research prototype over SEC filings and live market data: a compact typed-decision model (Laya) routes each question and screens out advice requests, Python computes every number, retrieval and tools fetch evidence, Mistral-7B writes a cited answer, a code validator checks that cited IDs exist and that numbers match computed notes, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server exposes the pipeline. In live experiments, Laya routed better than Mistral-7B (0.85 vs. 0.52; overall 0.86 vs. 0.68, McNemar p = 0.0003); a 12B Mistral decided no better, and DeepSeek-R1-8B decided better (0.79 vs. 0.68, p = 0.0192) but about 9.9 times more slowly. Mistral-7B computed 29% of 100 financial calculations correctly against 100% for Python, a live quote cut price error from 210% to 0.00%, and hybrid retrieval reached 76% Hit@5 on 50 filing questions. Yet in a live case study, both agent answers passed validation while describing AMD sample data under NVIDIA's and Alphabet's names. A controlled upper-bound study on the FinRank benchmark explains why: when one figure in the shared evidence is corrupted, self-consistency stays confident (agreement 0.55 to 0.59 while accuracy falls from 0.50 to 0.00), and a shared-evidence check (the kind our validator performs) catches 35% of the errors, whereas a check against the original passage catches 77% ($p = 5.96 \times 10^{-8}$); for DeepSeek-R1-8B, 68% vs. 90%. Verification must be independent of the evidence the writer saw.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.00986.title: HALO: Hierarchical Evidence Selection and Reinforcement Learning for Allocating Budgeted Label Optimization from Longitudinal Clinical Records
arXiv|arxiv:2611.00986.abstract: Learning from extensive longitudinal clinical records--spanning repeated encounters, evolving conditions, and heterogeneous documentation--under a finite labeling budget requires solving two coupled problems: deciding what evidence to keep and deciding which patients deserve higher-fidelity labels. Prior work on active learning and multi-fidelity label acquisition mainly addresses the second problem, while treating the evidence presented to the acquisition policy as fixed. We present HALO, a Hierarchical Evidence Selection and Reinforcement Learning pipeline for Allocating Budgeted Label Optimization from Longitudinal Clinical Records. This framework jointly learns what to read and what label source to acquire under budget. arXiv|arxiv:2609.21214.title: Ability-Residual Decoupled Modeling for Affective Cognitive Diagnosis
arXiv|arxiv:2609.21214.abstract: Cognitive diagnosis infers students' concept mastery from response logs. However, students' responses are not determined by mastery alone: non-cognitive factors such as emotion, engagement, and fatigue can also affect performance. Affective cognitive diagnosis therefore extends conventional cognitive diagnosis by incorporating affective states. Existing methods often assume that the cognitive diagnosis backbone has already explained ability, item, and concept effects, so the remaining errors can be attributed mainly to affect. We argue that this assumption can be insufficient in real educational data: item calibration bias, systematic concept bias, personalized student-concept deviations, and latent student-item matching can form stable cognitive residuals. Without an explicit modeling pathway, these residuals may leak into affective representations, producing affect contamination. The model first captures unmodeled cognitive residuals through student, item, concept, student-concept, and low-rank student-item components, and then uses an affective module to modulate guess/slip effects. A Q-matrix-constrained concept residual attention mechanism adaptively aggregates only item-relevant concept residuals. arXiv|arxiv:2604.16648.title: FRIGID: Scaling Diffusion-Based Molecular Generation from Mass Spectra at Training and Inference Time
arXiv|arxiv:2604.16648.abstract: Tandem mass spectrometry is prominent in scientific discovery workflows for identifying unknown small molecules, yet high-throughput structural elucidation remains challenging. While recent autoregressive and graph diffusion models have shown promise in de novo elucidation, performance remains limited by poor scalability during both training and inference time. In this work, we present FRIGID, a framework with a novel diffusion language model that generates molecular structures conditioned on mass spectra via intermediate fingerprint representations and determined chemical formulae, training at the scale of hundreds of millions of unlabeled structures. We then demonstrate how forward fragmentation models enable inference-time scaling by identifying spectrum-inconsistent fragments and refining them through targeted remasking and denoising. While FRIGID already achieves strong performance with its diffusion base, inference-time scaling significantly improves its accuracy, surpassing 18% Top-1 accuracy on the challenging MassSpecGym benchmark and tripling the Top-1 accuracy of the leading methods on NPLIB1. Further empirical analyses show that FRIGID exhibits log-linear performance scaling with increasing inference-time compute, opening a promising new direction for continued improvements in de novo structural elucidation. FRIGID code is publicly available at https://github.com/coleygroup/FRIGID.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.28558.title: From Reward Engineering to Data-Centric Reinforcement Learning for Effective Agentic Visual Tool Use
arXiv|arxiv:2611.28558.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) increasingly use external visual tools to acquire evidence during reasoning, yet learning when to invoke these tools remains challenging. Existing tool-use reinforcement learning (RL) methods often rely on call-contingent rewards to encourage beneficial tool use, but such reward engineering can distort the task objective and lead to degenerate calling behaviors. We argue that effective tool-use learning requires identifying not merely which questions are difficult, but which failures are attributable to missing visual evidence and can therefore be corrected through tool observations. We propose AOVO, a data-centric framework that enables MLLMs to learn effective tool use through perception attribution and policy-adaptive data sampling (PADS), without introducing tool-specific rewards. It counterfactually probes the model's reasoning states to identify observation-sensitive questions, distinguishing them from reasoning-dominated ones. PADS then periodically estimates category-level observation effects from recent policy rollouts and dynamically reallocates the training distribution toward questions where visual observations provide informative learning signals, while optimizing solely for final-answer correctness. Experiments across diverse visual perception and multimodal reasoning benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over competitive tool-use MLLMs, with causal analysis further validating the data-centric perspective for learning effective visual tool use.

ACL Anthology|https://aclanthology.org/2.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) based multi-agent systems (MAS) show strong potential for tackling complex tasks through collaborative intelligence. Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) based methods provide promising approaches for enhancing MAS self-training by generating synthetic data, using Q-values to estimate agent contributions. To address this discrepancy, we propose Data Influence-oriented Tree Search (DITS), a novel framework that incorporates influence scores to guide both tree search and data selection in data synthesis. arXiv|arxiv:2610.19789.title: More Methods, Better Agents? A Reality Check on Self-Distillation in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
arXiv|arxiv:2610.19789.abstract: Self-distillation in agentic reinforcement learning has produced a growing number of methods. However, existing evaluations often reuse published baseline scores under differing experimental conditions, provide few direct comparisons among contemporaneous methods, and give limited attention to training stability and computational cost. These limitations obscure the source of reported gains and the practical strengths and weaknesses of competing methods. Costly agent training further motivates a common basis for comparison. To address these gaps, we compare ten representative methods against GRPO on ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, Search-QA, and WebShop across three model sizes. Our study comprises 132 training runs totaling 12,124.4 recorded H800 GPU-hours, with repeated evaluations over eight rollout seeds for the pretrained backbones and all eleven trained methods. Beyond final task performance, we examine training progress, stability, and measured computational cost. Our evaluation yields three key findings. First, gains over GRPO remain limited in scope, with no method consistently outperforming it across settings. Second, strong final performance can mask unstable training. Third, additional training cost does not consistently translate into better performance. We establish this benchmark to support fair, comprehensive comparison and guide future research toward reliable and cost-effective improvements in agent training. arXiv|arxiv:2610.38155.title: Floor It, Then Fill It: Simulating Creator Ecosystems for Fair Video-Content Recommendation Systems at Billion User Scale
arXiv|arxiv:2610.38155.abstract: Engagement-optimized content recommendation systems exhibit a well-documented rich-get-richer dynamic that structurally disadvantages emerging creators on large-scale platforms. Evaluating debiasing interventions at scale demands faithful simulation of creator-viewer ecosystems, yet the fidelity, diversity, and validity of such simulators remain underexplored. We present a grounded user-simulation framework that models a heterogeneous population of ${\sim}42$K creators and their coupled viewer interactions over 12~weeks, and use it to evaluate equitable view-allocation policies formulated as a budgeted multi-armed bandit (MAB). The simulator captures three behavioral dimensions: (i)~\textbf{creator diversity}, modeled via a clustering approach grounded in real platform creator-level distributions; (ii)~\textbf{behavioral fidelity}, captured through coupled creator-content state machines that represent growth trajectories, engagement accumulation, and graduation dynamics; and (iii)~\textbf{population-level validity}, measured by calibration against observed platform metrics. We evaluate simulative-configurations that vary content-viewership target definitions, reward functions, and a small-creator reserve lever to maximize creator-content recommendation equity. A floor-protected per content-view-target with a view-parity-gap reward guarantees 90\% of view targets being met by creators every week, grows small-creator organic reach ${\sim}{+}33\%$ per week, and achieves high distribution stability (set of creators with funded-views Jaccard $= 0.819$). We analyze the Sim2Real gap and propose validation protocols, contributing evidence for when simulation-derived fairness conclusions can be trusted.

ACL Anthology|https://aclanthology.org/2.title: Consolidation or Adaptation? PRISM: Disentangling SFT and RL Data via Gradient Concentration
ACL Anthology|https://aclanthology.org/2.abstract: While Hybrid Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) followed by Reinforcement Learning (RL) has become the standard paradigm for training LLM agents, effective mechanisms for data allocation between these stages remain largely underexplored. Current data arbitration strategies often rely on surface-level heuristics that fail to diagnose intrinsic learning needs. Since SFT targets pattern consolidation through imitation while RL drives structural adaptation via exploration, misaligning data with these functional roles causes severe optimization interference. We propose PRISM, a dynamics-aware framework grounded in Schema Theory that arbitrates data based on its degree of cognitive conflict with the model’s existing knowledge. By analyzing the spatial geometric structure of gradients, PRISM identifies data triggering high spatial concentration as high-conflict signals that require RL for structural restructuring. In contrast, data yielding diffuse updates is routed to SFT for efficient consolidation. Extensive experiments on WebShop and ALFWorld demonstrate that PRISM achieves a Pareto improvement, outperforming state-of-the-art hybrid methods while reducing computational costs by up to 3.22 \times. Our findings suggest that disentangling data based on internal optimization regimes is crucial for scalable and robust agent alignment.

ACL Anthology|https://aclanthology.org/2.abstract: Modern coding agents are increasingly deployed for realistic software engineering, yet existing benchmarks primarily evaluate static, fixed-target tasks, failing to capture the long-horizon, multi-turn nature of real-world development. We introduce MACBench, a novel benchmark evaluating agents on sustained frontend web application development where text-based user requirements continuously evolve within a persistent workspace. Comprising 28 repository instances across 8 domains, MACBench features 699 dialogue turns and 956 evaluation items. It explicitly models realistic interaction patterns, challenging agents to maintain cross-turn coherence and continuous executability. Our dual-branch evaluation framework assesses both process robustness and final artifact quality, uniquely integrating intermediate viability checks with bounded runtime-feedback repair. Benchmarking 4 contemporary models reveals a severe reliability gap: the best-performing agent achieves only a 70.6% checklist success rate and a 10.7% strict instance success rate, struggling to satisfy requirements accumulated over long sessions. Furthermore, ablation studies reveal diminishing and sometimes negative returns from runtime-feedback repair: while it improves checklist success by an average of 10.4% and aids immediate failure recovery, excessive repair attempts frequently degrade final functional outcomes, suggesting they may introduce regressions or side effects in the evolving codebase. Finally, failure analysis identifies complex cross-turn application logic as the dominant bottleneck, accounting for 33–50% of unresolved errors.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.40016.title: LOGIV: Graph-Verified Execution with Causal Local Repair for Long-Horizon Robot Tasks
arXiv|arxiv:2610.40016.abstract: Agentic robots must turn a high-level goal into actions while keeping the physical conditions needed for future steps valid. A completed action does not ensure that its effects will persist: a later disturbance can invalidate support that the remaining plan still assumes. We present LOGIV, a graph engineering framework for agentic robot execution that uses an explicit task graph to connect symbolic planning, observation-based verification, and embodied action. LOGIV compiles a validated plan into condition-support and resource-ordering edges, checks their physical validity during execution, and uses dependency tracing to determine what must be restored after a failure. Repair is constrained by retained unfinished actions, and the combined continuation is symbolically validated before execution resumes. The framework operates above existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) and World Action Model (WAM) policies without adding trainable components. Across 20 dual-arm tasks from RoboTwin V2 and BiCoord with three execution backbones, LOGIV improves mean task success without injected disturbances by 10.67 and 15.33 percentage points, respectively. Under predefined perturbations, it achieves higher task completion and condition restoration than three adapted recovery baselines for every backbone on both benchmarks. On three real-robot tasks, successful trials increase from 12/30 to 17/30. These results support explicit, continuously checked task dependencies as a practical interface for reliable agentic robot execution.

arXiv|arxiv:2609.25634.title: An Exploratory Replica-Overlap Probe of the Grokking Transition
arXiv|arxiv:2609.25634.abstract: We trained 64 independently seeded networks in four configurations, continuing each to sustained convergence or a 40,000-epoch ceiling. We then asked whether an RSB-inspired distribution of pairwise weight overlaps changes across the grokking transition. It is the alignment step, not the overlap statistic, that determines what this registered probe can report. The registered implementation permutes hidden units without the corresponding bias and head-internal permutations and therefore does not preserve the network function. Every q_wt value computed through this alignment inherits the defect; q_fn does not, because it is computed from predictions of the unpermuted models. The numerical-precision requirement also failed, and an audit found protocol deviations. Consequently, the pre-registered rule gives no verdict: registered outcome UNDETERMINED (reason code C0_INSTRUMENT_INVALID). These data provide neither a confirmatory null nor a validated reading of the Parisi order parameter. Only frac40 cleared the 12/16 checkpoint-completeness requirement. For this configuration, a post-hoc criterion applied to the same data gave a Hartigan-dip interval containing zero (95% CI for Delta dip = [-0.017, 0.034]), whereas the overlap standard deviation increased by a factor of about 5.6. A post-hoc calibration assigns the dip test zero power at the simulated separations; the interval is therefore uninformative, not evidence of no change. The standard-deviation ratio is the only statistic here with power at the observed effect. Ensemble loss was near-flat only under the pre-specified 1% threshold. Finally, grokking rates of 0/16, 11/16 and 16/16 remain descriptive because train fraction is confounded with split identity.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.09708.title: A wearable input/output interface learns personalized models of haptic perception
arXiv|arxiv:2611.09708.abstract: Wearable haptic interfaces deliver physical stimuli to the skin, yet perceived locations vary widely across users and diverge from actuator locations, particularly for emergent tactile-feedback techniques. We developed a wearable haptic input/output (I/O) device integrating a 36-channel electrotactile array with capacitive touch sensing, enabling stimulation and user-reported percept locations to be registered within the same body-referenced coordinate frame. In 24 participants, the device revealed electrotactile and referred-thermal perceptual maps with notable interparticipant variability. Despite this variability, both modalities retained electrode-pair-specific spatial structure across participants. Tactile and thermal percepts also showed spatial correspondence, whose strength varied across participants. These findings motivated our human-in-the-loop calibration framework, which adapts a forward-prediction strategy to individual users and generates personalized perceptual models. These models enabled inverse rendering by selecting stimulation patterns predicted to generate a target percept for a specific user. Using these models, we demonstrate personalized haptic rendering in haptic-guided robot teleoperation, visual-to-haptic sensory substitution, interpersonal haptic communication, and virtual reality (VR). Together, this platform provides a route toward adaptive haptic interfaces that measure, model, and render according to each user's perception.

arXiv|arxiv:2609.22967.title: General Collaborative Intelligence: Architecting Cognition for Resilient Multi-Agent Ecosystems
arXiv|arxiv:2609.22967.abstract: Multi-agent unmanned systems are moving from isolated, ego-centric sensing toward collaborative intelligence, in which distributed agents exchange compact features to overcome a local observation trap that no single agent can escape: occlusions, finite sensor range, and environmental degradation. The field has matured across architectural, communication, embodied, resilience, and trust dimensions, yet existing surveys examine these dimensions in isolation and rarely expose their dependencies. This review offers a unified synthesis through two complementary lenses. The first is a five-dimensional taxonomy spanning collaboration stage, communication paradigm, fusion architecture, learning strategy, and application domain. The second is three cognitive synergy conditions, Semantic Disambiguation, Pragmatic Information Exchange, and Proactive Informational Foraging, that turn cognitive synergy into operational criteria. Across these lenses we survey collaboration architectures and topologies, neural-communication co-design that treats the channel as a differentiable pipeline component, embodied action-perception loops via multi-agent reinforcement learning, and resilience mechanisms for synchronization, uncertainty quantification, and label-efficient learning. We then map these advances onto four operational domains, V2X, unmanned aerial, industrial logistics, and smart cities, and onto the safety-privacy-utility triad. To counter benchmark saturation and evaluation fragmentation, we propose GCI-Bench, a five-pillar scoring protocol with a maturity model that makes the trade-offs of collaborative methods comparable across studies. A critical reflection on reproducibility, the sim-to-real gulf, and conditions under which collaboration degrades performance identifies open challenges and charts directions toward general collaborative intelligence under real-world uncertainty.

arXiv|arxiv:2609.39049.title: Structure vs. Chain-of-Thought: Evaluating LLM Criteria Extraction for Depression Severity
arXiv|arxiv:2609.39049.abstract: A large language model (LLM) can rate depression severity directly from a social media post, or mark which clinical criteria the post shows and let a simple rule turn the count into a label. The latter is easier to audit because a clinician can check each marked criterion. We compare these approaches on two Reddit corpora using three LLMs (from 9B to frontier scale) and two questionnaires (PHQ-9, BDI-II), and measure agreement with quadratic weighted kappa. For the two frontier models, criteria extraction scores above chain-of-thought on one corpus only when its decision thresholds are fitted on labeled data. Neither model's gain is significant, with or without recalibrating chain-of-thought on the same labels. With thresholds fixed a priori from PHQ-9's criteria, extraction shows no gain on either corpus, even where models mark over two criteria per post. The 9B model behaves differently on a corpus from depression communities. It labels most posts as severe, whether prompted directly or with chain-of-thought, while the a priori rule, which uses no labels, beats both. After chain-of-thought is recalibrated on the same labels, no significant gap remains, consistent with a calibration effect. Yet higher ordinal agreement does not ensure better detection of severe cases. PHQ-9 criteria extraction misses most severe posts, and moving from direct prompting to chain-of-thought and then to extraction increases misses in nearly all comparisons. On one corpus, a relabeled stress dataset, a model using that dataset's own features, some computed from the post text, is not significantly different from frontier criteria extraction under the a priori rule.

arXiv|arxiv:2606.08091.title: VideoWeaver: Evaluating and Evolving Skills for Agentic Long Video Generation
arXiv|arxiv:2606.08091.abstract: Agentic long video generation requires planning, tool orchestration, and cross-clip coordination over a long horizon. Most existing video agents either rely on static, human-crafted workflows, which require substantial manual effort and poorly adapt across tasks, or iteratively refine the output of the current task without persistently distilling execution experience into reusable skills for future tasks. We introduce VideoWeaver, an agent harness and benchmark that evaluates and evolves skills for long video generation. Given a single high-level instruction, an agent dynamically composes foundation skills into its own workflow rather than following a predefined pipeline. We construct a benchmark of 16 task categories and 285 cases, with references spanning text, image, audio, video, and their combinations. We further propose an evidence-grounded agent-as-judge that inspects both the execution trace and the final video to diagnose process and output failures. Based on this feedback, our evolution algorithm progressively refines category-level composition and creator skills, allowing recurring experience to guide dynamically constructed workflows for unseen cases. Experiments show that explicit composition skills improve the generation process over foundation skills alone, while skill evolution further improves output quality and generalizes to unseen cases. Incorporating judge feedback yields additional gains, especially on output metrics, and the agent-as-judge aligns well with human, particularly on process metrics. Code is available at https://github.com/JianhuiWei7/VideoWeaver.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.20954.title: Cross-subject decoding of imagined speech from scalp EEG: a leakage-controlled evaluation on three public corpora
arXiv|arxiv:2610.20954.abstract: Objective. A decoder of imagined speech that works for a new user without calibration would make a non-invasive speech interface practical. We tested whether imagined-speech content recorded with scalp electroencephalography (EEG) transfers across people, and examined why accuracy within a single person remains low. Approach. We analyzed three public corpora, ds003626, KaraOne and Track 3 of the 2020 International Brain-Computer Interface Competition, under a protocol that enforces split integrity by assertion and reports exact binomial thresholds, group tests and bootstrap confidence intervals. We trained decoders on each participant and tested them on every other, compared representational geometry across participants without a classifier, applied subject-level alignment, and tested five explanations for the within-subject ceiling. Main results. Across 482 ordered pairs of participants, no pair survived correction for multiple comparisons; mean pair-transfer accuracy lay within 0.006 of chance on every corpus, while every within-subject reference lay above it. Imagery against pre-stimulus rest generalized at about 0.61 after artifact and elapsed-time controls, but its decoder labelled the interval preceding imagery as imagery as often as imagery itself, so the contrast reflects a post-stimulus state, not imagery. Within subject, only the competition corpus decoded above threshold for every participant (0.3147; chance 0.200); syllable count explained little of this, but its frequency profile failed an artifact audit. Significance. In these corpora, imagined-speech content did not transfer between people through any representation we examined. Trial count per class was the only variable that ordered the corpora, which favors larger single-condition datasets over further model development.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.02616.title: VERSE: Verified Self-Evolving Optimizer for Agent Harnesses
arXiv|arxiv:2610.02616.abstract: Harness evolution improves an LLM agent's prompts, tools, and workflow, while the optimizer's own tools and procedures often remain fixed. We study whether an optimizer can improve another agent more effectively by also improving how it diagnoses failures, develops edits, and tests their effects. Two observations guide our design. In a controlled study, optimizer self-evolution fails to improve performance without execution-based verification, but achieves the best result of that study when verification is available. Across five executors, self-evolving optimizers build their own tools for failure analysis, verification, training audits, and workflow control. Motivated by these findings, we introduce VERSE, a Verified Self-Evolving optimizer for agent harnesses. VERSE lets the optimizer test draft edits, replay failures, and perturb suspected steps before submission, while tracking fixes and regressions across rounds. Using this feedback, the optimizer revises both the executor harness and its own prompts, skills, tools, hooks, and notes, while the weights of the optimizer and executor models stay fixed. Under a shared protocol with disjoint training, validation, and test tasks, VERSE improves all four evaluated harness optimizers on held-out SWE-rebench tasks and newer out-of-distribution tasks in five languages. Its best validation-selected harness reaches 42.3% and 37.7% accuracy, respectively, against 39.2% and 29.3% for the strongest baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/wzekai/VERSE.

arXiv|arxiv:2607.17780.title: ETAS: An Effect-Typed Language for Agent Systems
arXiv|arxiv:2607.17780.abstract: Agent systems are programs that coordinate language-model queries, tool calls, human approvals, and ordinary computation, yet existing frameworks wire them together as opaque library objects outside compiler analysis. Treating agent systems from a programming-language perspective, we present Etas, an effect-typed language that elevates agents, tools, workflows, and behavioral specifications to first-class, compiler-checked constructs. Crucially, Etas separates escaping effects from persistent effect request summaries: handlers change how an operation is interpreted without erasing its effect request from the summary, while trace specs constrain permitted effect requests and their order. The compiler composes effect request summaries across calls and handlers, discharging satisfied trace specs statically and keeping a residual monitor where dynamic paths remain uncertain. We formalize Core Etas with terminal handlers, a trace-spec monitor construction, and an abstract analysis over monitor states, proving preservation, progress, effect coverage, and trace-spec safety. We implement a compiler, an optimizer, and a checked interpreter using Rust. Across compiler fixtures and coding-agent scenarios written in Etas, Etas successfully enforces callable bounds, effect operation ordering, and handled effect request visibility with zero mismatches. The compiler also implements agent-specific optimizations that reduce execution time by 23.2%. Across 12 Etas workflows, the combined token optimization passes reduce input tokens by 67.8% on paired-correct executions. First-class agent abstractions also enable recursive self-evolution for Etas programs. Across five harness evolution iterations, task accuracy rises from 69.9% to 78.9%.

arXiv|arxiv:2603.11137.title: Scaling Reasoning Efficiently via Relaxed On-Policy Distillation
arXiv|arxiv:2603.11137.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a promising approach for transferring reasoning capabilities to capacity-constrained models, yet sampled-token OPD often suffers from entropy collapse and negative transfer. We identify uniform credit allocation as a key bottleneck: existing objectives obtain dense teacher feedback on student-generated trajectories, but apply it uniformly across sampled tokens despite highly heterogeneous token-level signals. Most tokens carry redundant near-zero credit, while rare heavy-tailed negative credits can dominate updates and prematurely suppress plausible reasoning trajectories. We introduce REOPOLD (Relaxed On-Policy Distillation), a framework that relaxes this uniform assignment by controlling where teacher feedback is applied, how strongly it affects the update, and when the allocation rule changes during training. Across diverse reasoning tasks, REOPOLD improves sampled-token OPD over recent post-training baselines with up to 12x higher sample efficiency, and extends to cross-vocabulary distillation, self-distillation, and test-time scaling.

arXiv|arxiv:2609.30662.title: LLM Parkinsonism: Executive-Control Failure, Token-Inefficient Persistence, and an Uncertainty-Aware Global Executive Control Architecture for Autonomous Language-Model Agents
arXiv|arxiv:2609.30662.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can plan, use tools, write code, and execute long-horizon workflows, yet strong local competence does not guarantee project-level executive control. Agents may continue acting after the original objective is satisfied, producing low-value refinements, repeated verification, and repairs to self-created complexity. We use LLM Parkinsonism as a narrowly defined, non-clinical metaphor for this pattern of persistent action despite diminishing task-level value. We argue that the problem is not explained by autoregressive next-token prediction alone, but more directly by concentrating proposal generation, scope interpretation, progress assessment, and stopping authority within the same self-conditioned loop. We therefore introduce Global Executive Control (GEC) v0.2, an uncertainty-aware governance architecture that separates action generation from project-level control. In a 24,000-episode matched-candidate benchmark under a common 40,000-token ceiling, a first-candidate baseline achieved 67.42% hard-goal success, a candidate-set local control achieved 96.53%, and GEC achieved 96.57%. The candidate-set control shows that access to multiple candidate actions explains most of the success gain; relative to that control, GEC preserved success while reducing mean token use from 19,782 to 12,574 (36.4%) and restricted mean tokens to completion at the 40,000-token ceiling from 16,136 to 13,114 (18.7%), while eliminating measured pre-completion drift and sharply reducing gross complexity. Governance-overhead sensitivity remained favorable through an additional 500 synthetic governance tokens per cycle. These mechanistic simulations support explicit governance of scope, evidence, resource use, and stopping, while live-model validation remains necessary.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.28315.title: Disclosure Begets Disclosure: A Self-Reinforcing Privacy Loop in LLM Agents with Persistent Memory
arXiv|arxiv:2610.28315.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly use persistent memory to personalize responses, and personal attributes in this memory pose a privacy risk if exposed. We ask how consulting memory during dialogue changes what users go on to say, and thus what the memory comes to reveal. In multi-session simulations, a simulated user with 24 personal attributes talks with a support agent that does or does not consult memory, and in both settings attributes are inferred from the full accumulated record. Across four support models, memory raises response quality but also empirical leakage, the share of attribute values correctly inferred from the record, by a margin that widens over sessions. The cause is a loop in ordinary, non-adversarial assistance. Memory-conditioned responses carry earlier values forward, often as presuppositions, and users affirm them or leave them uncorrected, so that cues and the agent's own guesses become recorded values. The loop reinforces itself, and removing the agent's mentions of an attribute lowers its later disclosure about twice as much as single-turn effects predict. Users cannot leave it on their own, since correcting a value discloses the attribute, declining to discuss it shifts later predictions toward sensitive values, and incorrect values left in place become entrenched. The loop is best weakened at the agent's response. Instructing the agent not to state or presuppose attributes brings leakage to about the no-memory level while keeping most of the quality gains, whereas filtering or anonymizing what users say or what is stored gives up much of them.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.26341.title: Reasoning on Call: Efficient Agentic Robot Control for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
arXiv|arxiv:2611.26341.abstract: Large multimodal models can support long-horizon robot manipulation, but frequent model calls incur substantial latency and token costs. The central challenge is determining when agent assistance or intervention is needed and whether errors require correcting robot execution, subtask planning, or both. To address this problem, we propose RoC (Reasoning on Call), an efficient framework that coordinates a low-level policy and a high-level reasoning agent through an online task-state monitor. The monitor combines temporal visual observations with ordered interaction memory to jointly estimate progress within the active subtask and predict its successor. These predictions guide event-triggered agent review for coordinated execution repair and plan revision. Verified outcomes govern memory updates and subtask transitions, allowing routine execution to remain with the policy while reasoning focuses on decisions requiring additional assessment. On RMBench, RoC improves task success rate by 24.0 percentage points and reduces token consumption by 65.3% compared with the strongest agent-based baseline. It also outperforms the strongest policy-based baseline by 15.1 percentage points in task success rate. Real-world experiments further validate its effectiveness across three long-horizon manipulation tasks. abstract: Large multimodal models can support long-horizon robot manipulation, but frequent model calls incur substantial latency and token costs. The central challenge is determining when agent assistance or intervention is needed and whether errors require correcting robot execution, subtask planning, or both. To address this problem, we propose RoC (Reasoning on Call), an efficient framework that coordinates a low-level policy and a high-level reasoning agent through an online task-state monitor. The monitor combines temporal visual observations with ordered interaction memory to jointly estimate progress within the active subtask and predict its successor. These predictions guide event-triggered agent review for coordinated execution repair and plan revision. Verified outcomes govern memory updates and subtask transitions, allowing routine execution to remain with the policy while reasoning focuses on decisions requiring additional assessment. On RMBench, RoC improves task success rate by 24.0 percentage points and reduces token consumption by 65.3% compared with the strongest agent-based baseline. It also outperforms the strongest policy-based baseline by 15.1 percentage points in task success rate. Real-world experiments further validate its effectiveness across three long-horizon manipulation tasks. Overall, RoC supports efficient agent intervention and coordinated recovery across execution and planning for long-horizon robot manipulation.

arXiv|arxiv:2603.14681.abstract: Bayesian change-point and segmentation models provide uncertainty-aware piecewise-constant representations of ordered data, but exact inference is often limited to narrow likelihood classes, single sequences, or index-uniform designs. For non-conjugate GLM blocks, the same DP layer can use deterministic local approximations such as Laplace, variational methods, EP, or quadrature. We prove a posterior-odds stability bound: uniform per-block log-evidence error ε perturbs k-odds and boundary-odds by at most (k+k')ε and 2kε. arXiv|arxiv:2601.14969.title: Robust Machine Learning for Regulatory Sequence Modeling under Biological and Technical Distribution Shifts
arXiv|arxiv:2601.14969.abstract: Robust machine learning for regulatory genomics is studied under biologically and technically induced distribution shifts. Deep convolutional and attention-based models achieve strong in-distribution performance on DNA regulatory sequence prediction tasks but are usually evaluated under i.i.d. assumptions, even though real applications involve cell type-specific programs, evolutionary turnover, assay protocol changes, and sequencing artifacts. We introduce a robustness framework that combines a mechanistic simulation benchmark with real data analysis on an MPRA dataset to quantify performance degradation, calibration failures, and uncertainty-based reliability. In simulation, motif-driven regulatory outputs are generated with cell type-specific programs, PWM perturbations, GC bias, depth variation, batch effects, and heteroscedastic noise, and CNN, BiLSTM, and transformer models are evaluated. Models remain accurate and reasonably calibrated under mild GC content shifts but show higher error, severe variance miscalibration, and coverage collapse under motif effect rewiring and noise-dominated regimes, revealing robustness gaps invisible to standard i.i.d. evaluation. Adding simple biological structural priors, motif-derived features in simulation, and global GC content in MPRA improves distribution error and yields consistent robustness gains under biologically meaningful genomic shifts, while providing only limited protection against strong assay noise. Uncertainty-aware selective prediction offers an additional safety layer, and risk coverage analyses on simulated and MPRA data show that filtering low-confidence inputs recovers low-risk subsets, including under GC-based OOD conditions, although reliability gains diminish when noise dominates.

PMLR|https://proceedings.mlr.press/v300/.title: Scalable Utility-Aware Multiclass Calibration
PMLR|https://proceedings.mlr.press/v300/.abstract: Ensuring that classifiers are well-calibrated, i.e., their predictions align with observed frequencies, is a minimal and fundamental requirement for classifiers to be viewed as trustworthy. Existing methods for assessing multiclass calibration often focus on specific aspects associated with prediction (e.g., top-class confidence, class-wise calibration) or utilize computationally challenging variational formulations. In this work, we study scalable \emph{evaluation} of multiclass calibration. To this end, we propose utility calibration, a general framework which measures the calibration error relative to a specific utility function that encapsulates the goals or decision criteria relevant to the end user. We demonstrate how this framework can unify and re-interpret several existing calibration metrics, particularly allowing for more robust versions of the top-class and class-wise calibration metrics, and going beyond such binarized approaches, towards assessing calibration for richer classes of downstream utilities.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.03213.title: Toward SLM-based agentic task-tool intent matching
arXiv|arxiv:2610.03213.abstract: Tool-equipped AI agents use tool calls to access data and act on external systems. Horizontal growth of agentic systems increases the number of these interactions, and further motivates the need for automated, per-call oversight that can operate at low latency and/or on-prem. Conventional authorization schemes can determine whether an agent is allowed to invoke a tool, but cannot assess the agent's underlying cognition, specifically, whether the tool selection represents a logical, relevant step toward satisfying the intent of the task or not. Consequently, an allowed call may still deviate from the task's intent: a rogue agent might deviate the calls or nudge other agents to make a combination of calls that would not align with the intent of the task. Therefore, every call needs to be verified. In this study we investigate the applicability of Small Language Models (SLMs) to this purpose: an SLM functions as a task-tool relevance classifier that evaluates every selected tool independently against the assigned task and returns a relevance signal for downstream enforcement. Equipped with a novel dataset with multi-tool tasks whose required tools span distinct Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, we used prompt-optimization, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning through GRPO to optimize and specialize SLMs.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.33036.title: Towards Realistic Evaluation of Uncertainty Quantification for LLM-Based Recommender Systems
arXiv|arxiv:2611.33036.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) provide a flexible interface for recommendation systems. However, their issued rankings require reliable instance-level uncertainty monitoring. In this scenario, comparing uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods becomes challenging because LLM rankers lack a standard item-classification head. Their scores may depend on option labels, prompts, generation procedures, and the available user and item evidence. Existing methods derive uncertainty from different sources and apply it at different stages of the recommendation process. Some methods evaluate an issued ranking, whereas others use uncertainty to change the ranking itself, making direct comparison difficult. Here we introduce a fixed-ranking benchmark which evaluates eight heterogeneous UQ signals as record-level monitors under a shared output contract. We evaluate these signals across four recommendation datasets and two LLM backbones under a shared fixed-ranking protocol. From the results, we draw three main observations. First, UQ method ordering changes across backbones even on the same reference instances. Second, ranking-aligned Top10Mass provides the strongest scalar Error@10 detection in several evaluation conditions, reflecting effective cutoff-aligned monitoring, while its advantage narrows for popularity-tail targets. Third, scalar UQ signals are weak at identifying which control has the larger clipped NDCG@10 difference, whereas source-specific signals, including Perturbation Rank Instability and simple listwise distances, provide stronger paired-control agreement, reflecting their sensitivity to the two controlled evidence sources. These findings motivate us to evaluate ranking-failure detection, robustness across recommendation conditions, and responses to controlled evidence changes as distinct properties of UQ.

arXiv|arxiv:2609.21340.title: Conformal Privacy Auditing: Calibrated Re-identification Attacks with Statistical Guarantees
arXiv|arxiv:2609.21340.abstract: Empirical identity leakage from released text is increasingly driven by attackers that combine large language models (LLMs) with auxiliary knowledge to link documents to individuals. Existing audits typically report success rates for specific attack pipelines but lack finite-sample statistical guarantees, while training-time protections such as differential privacy are difficult to translate into release-time decisions for individual natural-language documents. We introduce Conformal Privacy Auditing(CPA), a distribution-free calibration framework that provides a statistical certificate of re-identification risk for each released document against LLM-empowered adversaries. CPA outputs a conformal ambiguity set of candidate identities that is guaranteed to contain the true identity with user-chosen confidence under exchangeability, together with an interpretable leakage proxy derived from set size. CPA supports both logit-access and sampling-only attackers, enabling audits of open-source models and proprietary API models in a unified framework. Across multiple release benchmarks and attacker configurations, CPA achieves calibrated coverage and reveals sharp shifts in certified identifiability as auxiliary knowledge, LLM augmentation, and release mechanisms vary, providing a statistically grounded basis for reporting and comparing release-time linkage risk across attacker configurations, datasets, and release mechanisms alike.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.12386.title: Say Shibboleth: Fingerprinting the LLMs and Harnesses Behind Agentic Attacks
arXiv|arxiv:2611.12386.abstract: We study the fingerprinting of agentic cyberattacks. Our objective is to reliably infer information about the attacker's configuration, such as LLM version and harness, from telemetry. To achieve this, we introduce a technique we call shibboleth traps: modular honeypot services designed to elicit discriminative behaviors from agentic attackers. The traps make informative interactions a condition for obtaining resources the agent seeks, eliciting model declarations and characteristic writing without requiring a successful prompt injection. To achieve harness fingerprinting, we introduce general mechanisms to indirectly probe peculiar execution behaviors of harnesses. These probes reveal how a harness masks secrets in tool output, enforces command time limits, and schedules tool calls, using only the effects visible in subsequent requests. We show that combined declarative and behavioral inference distinguishes among 15 candidate models with an average 90% top-1 accuracy, with behavioral classifiers evaluated on held-out harnesses or task families. In a separate experiment across four harnesses, fixed probe rules identify the correct harness with 92% accuracy. When instructed to conceal their identity, agents still leave useful behavioral evidence even as their declarations become uninformative.

OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.title: CocoRNA: Collective RNA Design with Cooperative Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning
OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: Designing RNA sequences that reliably fold into specific secondary structures is essential for understanding their biological functions but remains a challenging computational problem. We propose CocoRNA, a cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for RNA inverse design. CocoRNA simplifies the design task by decomposing it into smaller sub-problems, each solved collaboratively by multiple agents. This approach reduces the complexity of the problem and improves the exploration of design policies. During training, a centralized critic uses global structural information to guide the agents, enabling them to jointly optimize their design strategies. As a result, CocoRNA learns high-quality RNA design policies that generalize effectively to unseen structures without additional training. Experiments on the Rfam dataset demonstrate that CocoRNA substantially outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both success rate and design speed. Further experiments on other biological sequence design tasks highlight the effectiveness and broad potential of CocoRNA for complex design tasks.
